title: Kikalayi
author: Ssalongo Ssali
desc: Pork skin and fat rendered down first in a heavy pan until they give up their own oil, then the meat fried in that fat and stirred continuously — no added cooking oil at any point.
longDesc: Kikalayi is named after the pan: a big heavy frying pan built to spread heat evenly, and the dish is named for the vessel rather than the meat. The technique is what makes it a real dish rather than just fried pork. You separate the skin and fat from the muscle, render them first over moderate heat until they are brown and crunchy, and then fry the meat in the fat they released — which is why no oil goes into the pan. It belongs to Kampala's pork zones and the social life around them.
ingredients: 900 g (2 lb) pork, with the skin and fat on
steps: Cut the pork into substantial chunks, then separate the skin and fat from the muscle. Cut both into pieces.
Put the skin and fat in the large pan over moderate heat and render them for about 30 minutes, until brown and crunchy and swimming in their own oil. Add no cooking oil at all.
Add the meat pieces and cook them together with the skin, stirring continuously so they brown evenly and nothing catches.
Add the garlic, then the onions, and let them soften.
Add the green pepper, carrots and the potatoes if you are using them.
Add the tomatoes, cabbage, salt, pepper and curry powder, and stir well.
Add the water, bring to a simmer, and cook for close to an hour until the liquid has reduced to a cup or less.
chefTips: Render the skin and fat first and never add oil. That step is the dish — it produces all the cooking fat you need and it is why kikalayi tastes the way it does.
Stir continuously. Fat renders unevenly and a pan left alone will burn on the bottom while the top is still raw.
Moderate heat for the rendering, not high. You want the fat to run out slowly, not to seize and scorch.
Thirty minutes for the skin to go brown and crunchy is about right, and it is worth waiting for.

There are two accounts of the finished texture: a dry crisp fry with the meat's own flavour foregrounded, and a wetter hour-long simmer with vegetables. The restaurant version served in Kampala is the vegetable one, which is what this follows — but the dry version is real and is the purist's.
Traditional versions keep the seasoning minimal so the pork leads. Salt, pepper and garlic is plenty.
The vegetables go in near the end. Earlier and they disappear.
commonMistakes: Frying the meat and the skin together from the start, so the fat never renders properly.
Adding the vegetables at the beginning.
sources: The defining technique — separating skin and fat from the muscle, rendering them first over moderate heat so no additional cooking oil is needed, and stirring continuously — is documented in the encyclopedia entry for kikalayi, along with the etymology from the large frying pans it is cooked in.
Quantities adapted from 'Kikalayi Pork — Kampala Sanctuary Recipe', Purpose Jewelry, which names the organisation but no individual contributor.

The vegetable-inclusive version is supported by Kampala restaurant menus listing kikalayi style with cabbage and vegetables; the dry-crisp version comes from the encyclopedia description. The two accounts differ and the tips say so.
reheating: Warm in a pan — it reheats better than most fried pork because of the fat.
healthBenefits: Pork supplies protein, thiamine, selenium and zinc.
Cabbage, carrots, tomatoes and peppers go in the same pan.
Cooked entirely in its own rendered fat, so nothing is added — but it is a high-fat dish and honest about it.
culturalNote: Kampala's pork joints are a social institution rather than restaurants, and kikalayi is what they are built around. That the dish is named after the pan says something true about it: the vessel spreads the heat evenly enough to render and fry in one go, and without it you are cooking something else.
